justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the prevailing price level of roughly $370–372 for whatever underlying asset this represents (likely SPY or a similar broad equity index ETF given the price range). At the one-day horizon, I placed the estimate at $371.5, essentially assuming mean-reversion and continuity from the last observed price with minimal drift. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $373, reflecting a small positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run equity risk premium and the absence of any dominant near-term catalyst I could identify as clearly bearish. At the one-month horizon, I moved to $375, incorporating a slightly larger expected drift over a longer compounding window while recognizing that monthly returns historically skew modestly positive in the absence of a recession or shock.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility assumptions appropriate to each time horizon. Daily volatility for a broad equity index ETF tends to run around 0.8–1.2%, which translates to roughly a ±1.5–2% band at 90% confidence for a single day, consistent with my ±$13.5 range at one day. As the horizon extends to one week, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the band to roughly ±$25. At one month, the interval widens further to ±$45, reflecting not just scaled volatility but also the increased probability of regime-shifting events over a longer window.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy surprise, a significant deterioration in economic data suggesting recession, a geopolitical escalation, or a credit market disruption could easily produce drawdowns of 5–10% or more, breaking through the lower bounds of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish Fed pivot, a strong earnings season, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could produce a sharp rally exceeding the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions and options market positioning can also amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest, particularly around key macro data releases or central bank meetings that may fall within the forecast window.
